title: Oklahoma M3+ earthquakes fell faster after 2016 than pressure models fit to 2010-2016 disposal data predicted; pressure loss in 1-4 years was necessary and a memory term gave inconsistent gains
abstract: Question: after the 2015-2016 cuts in wastewater disposal, does the Oklahoma earthquake rate follow the pressure level, the pressure increase, a pressure history with memory (Kaiser type), or a pressure that dissipates? Approach: we used monthly volumes of 4,545 Class II disposal wells (OCC Form 1012A, 2006-2025) and declustered USGS ComCat M>=3 events inside Oklahoma (Zaliapin and Ben-Zion nearest-neighbour method). A 2-D diffusion model on 0.05 degree cells gave a pressure proxy with diffusivity D and optional loss time L. Each model had a shrunk productivity for each cell. We fit the models on 2010-2016 (1,317 events) and forecast 2017-01 to 2026-10 (423 events). We repeated this with fits to 2018 and to 2026, and with sensitivity variants. Results: all models fit to 2010-2016 predicted too many events. The closed pressure-level model predicted 16 times the observed count, rate-state with closed pressure 5.6 times, pressure-increase (seismogenic index) and Kaiser models 2.7 times, and the leaky pressure-level model 2.4 times. Pressure loss with an e-folding time of 1-4 years was necessary in all fit windows. The leaky level model was better than the pressure-increase and Kaiser models by 0.58 nats per event in 2017-2026 (95% cell bootstrap 0.40-0.77) and by 2.57 (2.07-3.05) when fit to 2018. A hysteresis factor (p/p_max)^n gave inconsistent gains across four designs (+0.33, -0.23, +0.28, +0.14 nats per event). With Arbuckle-labelled volumes it gave near-correct counts (493 for 423 events; 178 for 141), but with all disposal volumes the full-period fit selected n = 0.16. A seismic-depletion factor had no support. Even the full-period leaky fit expected 1.7 times the 96 events of 2020-2026. Declustered M>=3 events fell from 501 in 2015 to 5 in 2025. Limitations: single-layer linear diffusion, no poroelastic stress, no injection depth or plug-back information, no Kansas or Texas wells, uncertain formation labels, and many compared models without correction for selection.

All forecasts from 2016 are too high after 2017, except the hysteresis model with Arbuckle volumes.
Predicted/observed counts with 95% Poisson intervals for each model and design (A: fit 2010-2016; B: fit 2010-2018; C: full-period fit, in-sample 2020-2026). Values above 1 are over-predictions.
